chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, regarding the blood money (diya),

he said: 'A thousand dinars, or ten thousand dirhams; and from the owners of garments, garments are taken; and from the owners of camels, camels are taken; and from the owners of sheep, sheep; and from the owners of cattle, cattle.'

key_terms.الدِّيَة: Diya — blood money; the financial compensation owed to the victim's family for homicide or serious bodily injury
key_terms.الْإِبِل: Ibil — camels; a primary unit of wealth and the original basis of diya calculation
key_terms.الْبَقَر: Baqar — cattle/cows; accepted as a form of diya payment
key_terms.الْغَنَم: Ghanam — sheep and goats; small livestock accepted as diya payment
key_terms.حُلَل: Hulul (pl. of hullah) — fine robes or garments; a recognized form of wealth in classical Arabia
key_terms.دِرْهَم: Dirham — silver currency; ten thousand dirhams equates to one thousand dinars as the standard blood money
key_terms.دِينَار: Dinar — gold currency used in classical Islamic economy

ai.seo_question: What is the amount of blood money (diya) in Shia Islamic law according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This hadith narrated through a chain of highly trusted Shia transmitters specifies the amount and acceptable forms of diya (blood money) in Islamic law. The Imam (AS) establishes the equivalence of one thousand gold dinars or ten thousand silver dirhams, and specifies that payment may be made in kind — in garments, camels, sheep, or cattle — according to what the responsible party possesses. This ruling reflects the practical flexibility of Islamic jurisprudence in the context of early Arabian pastoral economies, where wealth was measured in livestock and trade goods.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, 
(It has been narrated) from Jameel Bin Darraj regarding the wergild, he<sup>asws</sup> (6<sup>th</sup> Imam<sup>asws</sup>) said: ‘

A thousand Dinar, or ten thousand Dirhams, and the garments would be seized from the owner of the garments, and the camels would be seized from the owners of the camels, and the sheep from the owners of the sheep, and the cows from the owners of the cows’.
